title: Sell Mineral Rights in Westover, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Westover, WV | Monongalia County
metaDescription: Westover sits across the river from Morgantown in an actively drilled part of Monongalia County. We trace the deed record and buy mineral interests.
heroLead: Westover sits directly across the Monongahela from Morgantown, in a stretch of Monongalia County that's seen real Marcellus horizontal development over the past decade, which changes how a mineral interest here should be valued.
intro: Monongalia County has drawn steady horizontal drilling activity as operators worked laterals into the Marcellus shale across the county, including areas close to Westover and the Morgantown metro footprint. That activity means a Westover-area mineral interest is often tied to modern production rather than only an old shallow well from decades ago.

We start by pulling the Monongalia County record to trace who currently holds the mineral interest under a specific Westover tract, whether it's leased, and whether it's part of a spacing unit that's producing or permitted.

sections.heading: Monongalia County's Horizontal Drilling Push
paragraphs: Operators have run multi-well pads and horizontal laterals through parts of Monongalia County for years now, and tracts around Westover have been swept into spacing units alongside adjoining farmland as development moved through the area. Whether your specific interest sits inside one of those units matters more to its value than the county name on the deed.
We check unit and permit records directly rather than relying on secondhand information from a neighbor or an old conversation with a landman.

sections.heading: Westover's Place Along the Monongahela
paragraphs: The land here is a mix of older residential development close to the river and outlying tracts that were still farmland when Marcellus leasing first came through the county. The mineral rights under both types of parcel were frequently severed from the surface at different points, sometimes generations apart, which affects how the chain of title reads.
We treat each Westover file individually rather than assuming a uniform history across the town.

sections.heading: Converting a Flat-Rate Lease Near Morgantown
paragraphs: Some older leases on Monongalia County tracts near Westover were signed as flat-rate agreements before horizontal drilling made the underlying minerals significantly more valuable. If a well now produces under a spacing unit covering one of these tracts, the lease should have converted to at least the state's 1/8 statutory royalty floor.
We verify whether that conversion actually happened before we make an offer, since a mispriced flat-rate interest and a properly converted royalty interest aren't worth the same thing.

sections.heading: Fractional Interests From Old Mon County Farms
paragraphs: It's common for a Westover-area mineral interest to be held by several heirs of a farm family that owned the land before the area developed into its current mix of residential and commercial use. Those undivided fractions rarely get formally divided, even after decades of new owners inheriting a piece of the same original tract.
We buy individual fractional shares directly, and we do the work of confirming your specific percentage through the county record rather than asking you to sort that out first.

faqs.question: Is my mineral interest near Westover part of a producing spacing unit?
faqs.answer: We check the Monongalia County record along with permit and unit filings to confirm whether your specific tract is included in a producing or permitted unit before making an offer.

faqs.question: How do I know how large my fractional share is?
faqs.answer: We trace your interest through the deed and estate record to confirm your exact fraction, which is part of the title work we do before quoting a number.

faqs.question: My lease is old and flat-rate. Does that matter if there's a producing well nearby now?
faqs.answer: It can. If a well is producing under a unit that includes your tract, the lease may be required to convert to at least West Virginia's 1/8 statutory royalty, and we check this before valuing the interest.
